Figure 6. Driving force for dendritic cracking Finite element modeling (FEM) was used to compare charging protocols with (A) and without (B) current holds. For each case, the pressure buildup rate (ṗ) is assumed to be proportional to the charging current density (shown schematically for both cases), and the energy driving force (Gnet) is then the strain energy release rate obtained from the FEM (see Methods). The zero-current steps here correspond to fixing the pressure for a few hours, and this leads to significant relaxation of the driving force for dendritic cracking.

figures.caption: Figure S13. Geometry of the simulation and model setting of Video S4. The perfectly elastic-plastic model employed in this video assumes that plastic deformation occurs instantly upon yielding irrespective of deformation speed or strain rate. This is a valid assumption according to rate-dependent plastic FEM simulation of higher yield strength cases (4, 8, and 16 MPa) shown in Video S1–S3. As a result, this model does not explicitly capture the kinetics or rate effects of lithium’s plastic deformation, but reveals the full closure of the interfacial void for lithium-SE contact.
